dryRun.title: Find 7 in [4, 9, 7, 2]
dryRun.note: The scan stops at the first match. In the worst case (target is last, or missing) it looks at all n items: O(n).

think.q: console.log([4, 9, 7, 2].indexOf(7))
why: indexOf is a linear search. It returns the position of the first match, not the value.
The value 7 sits at index 2.

think.q: console.log([1, 2, 3].indexOf(5))
why: When nothing matches, indexOf returns -1. Index 0 is a real position, so it cannot mean "missing".
Your own search function should follow the same rule.

think.q: console.log([NaN].indexOf(NaN), [NaN].includes(NaN))
why: indexOf compares with ===, and NaN === NaN is false. So it never finds NaN.
includes uses "same value zero", which treats NaN as equal to itself.

think.q: What is the worst-case time of a linear search over n unsorted items?
why: If the target is last or missing, every item is checked once: O(n).
On unsorted data nothing faster is possible, because any unchecked item could be the target.

think.q: Which case is a good fit for a plain linear scan?
opts: Searching a sorted array of 10 million items thousands of times
Searching a small or unsorted array once
Looking up users by id inside a loop of 100,000 calls
Searching a sorted array for the first value that is at least x
why: One search on unsorted or tiny data is cheap, and sorting first would cost more than the scan.
For many searches, build a hash map (O(1) each) or keep the data sorted and use binary search.

try.task: Write findLast(nums, target). Return the last index where target appears, or -1 if it is not there. Do not use lastIndexOf.
try.hint: Walk from the end, i = nums.length - 1 down to 0, and return the first index that matches.

takeaway.key: Linear search checks items one by one: O(n) time, O(1) space. It is the right answer for unsorted or tiny data, and the baseline that faster methods must beat.
mistakes: Returning 0 for "not found" (0 is a real index). Use -1.
Using indexOf to look for NaN.
Scanning again and again inside a loop, which quietly makes the whole solution O(n²).
Forgetting that the scan can stop at the first match.

dryRun.title: Find 38 in [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56]
dryRun.note: Eight items took three looks. Each look throws away half of what is left, so n items need about log₂(n) looks.

think.q:
let lo = 0, hi = 7
const mid = lo + Math.floor((hi - lo) / 2)
console.log(mid)
why: The middle of 0 and 7 is 3.5, and Math.floor rounds it down to 3.
Writing lo + (hi - lo) / 2 instead of (lo + hi) / 2 is a habit from languages where lo + hi can overflow.

think.q:
function bs(a, t) {
  let lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1
  while (lo < hi) {
    const m = (lo + hi) >> 1
    if (a[m] === t) return m
    if (a[m] < t) lo = m + 1
    else hi = m - 1
  }
  return -1
}
console.log(bs([5], 5))
why: With one item, lo and hi are both 0, so lo < hi is false and the loop never runs. The item is never checked.
Fix: use lo <= hi. When the two meet, there is still one candidate left to check.

think.q:
console.log(Math.ceil(Math.log2(1000000)))

Binary search on 1,000,000 sorted items needs at most about how many looks?
why: Halving 1,000,000 down to 1 takes about 20 steps, because 2²⁰ is just over a million.
A linear scan could need a million looks. That gap is the whole point.

think.q: What must be true about the data before binary search works?
opts: It must have an even length
It must be sorted (or otherwise monotonic)
why: Discarding half is only safe when the order tells you which half cannot hold the target.
Duplicates and odd lengths are fine. On unsorted data the answer is simply wrong.

think.q: Inside while (lo <= hi) you write lo = mid instead of lo = mid + 1. When can the loop run forever?
opts: When lo equals mid and the target is bigger than arr[mid]
Never, the two are the same
Only when the array is empty
Only when the target is found
why: If lo === mid (for example lo = 4, hi = 5, so mid = 4) then lo = mid changes nothing, and the same range repeats forever.
You already checked mid, so always step past it: lo = mid + 1 or hi = mid - 1.

try.task: Write binarySearch(nums, target). nums is sorted in increasing order. Return the index of target, or -1. It must run in O(log n).
try.hint: Keep lo and hi as the inclusive range that can still hold the target. Loop while lo <= hi, look at mid, and move one boundary past mid.

checks.verify: assert(binarySearch([1, 3, 5, 7], 1) === 0 && binarySearch([1, 3, 5, 7], 7) === 3, "first or last item missed")

const big = Array.from({ length: 1000000 }, (_, i) => i * 2); const t0 = Date.now(); const r = binarySearch(big, 777778); assert(r === 388889 && Date.now() - t0 < 50, "wrong or too slow, did you scan the array?")

takeaway.key: On sorted data, look at the middle and throw away half each time: O(log n) time, O(1) space. Keep an inclusive range and always step past mid.
mistakes: Using lo < hi and skipping the last candidate.
Setting lo = mid or hi = mid and looping forever.
Running it on unsorted data.
Mixing the two styles: an inclusive hi = n - 1 with an exclusive loop condition.

dryRun.title: First index with a value ≥ 5 in [1, 3, 5, 5, 5, 8, 9]  (hi starts at n = 7)
rows: hi = 3, mid could be the answer
dryRun.note: The array looks like F F T T T T T. We are not looking for a value, we are looking for the first T. When the test is true, hi = mid (keep mid); when false, lo = mid + 1.

think.q:
function lb(a, t) {
  let lo = 0, hi = a.length
  while (lo < hi) {
    const m = (lo + hi) >> 1
    if (a[m] >= t) hi = m
    else lo = m + 1
  }
  return lo
}
const a = [1, 3, 5, 5, 5, 8, 9]
console.log(lb(a, 5), lb(a, 6), lb(a, 10))
why: lb(a, 5) is the first 5, at index 2. lb(a, 6) is where 6 would go: before the 8, at index 5.
Nothing is ≥ 10, so the answer is a.length = 7, one past the end.

think.q: In the "first index ≥ target" search, no value is ≥ the target. What should it return?
why: The answer is the insertion position, and a value bigger than everything belongs at the end: index nums.length.
This is why hi starts at n and not n - 1.

think.q: The array is sorted: [1, 3, 5, 5, 5, 8, 9]. How do you count the 5s in O(log n)?
opts: Scan from the first 5 to the last 5
Binary search for any 5 and double it
First index with a value > 5, minus first index with a value ≥ 5
why: The first index with a value > 5 is 5, and the first with a value ≥ 5 is 2. The difference, 3, is the count.
Two boundary searches give the whole run of equal values without walking it.

think.q:
const piles = [3, 6, 7, 11]
const hours = (k) => piles.reduce((s, p) => s + Math.ceil(p / k), 0)
console.log(hours(4), hours(3))

This is "minimum eating speed". What do these two numbers tell you?
why: At speed 4 it takes 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8 hours. At speed 3 it takes 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 hours.
A faster speed never takes longer, so "can finish in h hours" goes F F F T T T. That is a boundary, and we can binary search it even though no array exists.

think.q: You are finding the first index where the test is true. The test is true at mid. What do you do?
why: mid passes, but an earlier index might pass too. So keep mid inside the range: hi = mid.
If the test is false, mid cannot be the answer, so lo = mid + 1.

try.task: Write lowerBound(nums, target). nums is sorted. Return the first index i with nums[i] >= target, or nums.length if there is none.
try.hint: Start with lo = 0, hi = nums.length. While lo < hi: if nums[mid] >= target then hi = mid, else lo = mid + 1. Return lo.

checks.t: the first of several equal values

takeaway.key: Picture the data as F F F T T T and binary search for the first T. If the test is true use hi = mid, otherwise lo = mid + 1. The same idea works on an answer range, not only on arrays.
mistakes: Using hi = mid - 1 when the test is true, which can skip the answer.
Starting hi at n - 1, so "not found" cannot return n.
Returning -1 instead of the insertion position.
Using a test that is not monotonic (it must flip only once).

dryRun.title: Insertion sort on [5, 2, 4, 1]
dryRun.note: The part to the left of i is always sorted. Each round takes the next item (the key) and slides it left to its place. A nearly sorted array needs few shifts.

think.q:
const a = [3, 1, 2]
let shifts = 0
for (let i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {
  const key = a[i]
  let j = i - 1
  while (j >= 0 && a[j] > key) {
    a[j + 1] = a[j]
    j--
    shifts++
  }
  a[j + 1] = key
}
console.log(a.join(","), shifts)
why: Key 1 shifts the 3 once: [1, 3, 2]. Key 2 shifts the 3 once: [1, 2, 3]. That is 2 shifts.
Count the shifts and you know the work. Fewer shifts means a faster run.

think.q: What is the time of insertion sort on an array that is already sorted?
why: Each key is compared once with its left neighbour and stays. That is n - 1 cheap steps.
The worst case (reverse order) is O(n²), because every key slides all the way to the front.

think.q: In the shifting loop you change a[j] > key to a[j] >= key. What happens?
why: With >=, a key slides past an equal item, so equal items swap their original order.
Stable means equal items keep their order. It matters when you sort objects by one field and want the earlier order kept for ties.

think.q: console.log([10, 9, 1].sort().join(","))
why: Without a compare function, sort turns items into strings and compares those. "10" comes before "9".
Always pass one: nums.sort((a, b) => a - b).

think.q: When is insertion sort a good choice?
opts: A tiny or nearly sorted array
An array that must never be changed
A linked list of a million items
why: It has almost no overhead, and it is O(n) when little is out of place. Real sort routines use it for small chunks.
On a huge random array its O(n²) loses to O(n log n) sorts.

try.task: Write insertionSort(nums). Return a new sorted array in increasing order using insertion sort. The input must stay unchanged.
try.hint: Copy the array. For each i from 1: save key = a[i], then while the left neighbour is bigger, shift it right. Finally drop the key into the gap.

checks.verify: const x = [3, 1, 2]; insertionSort(x); assert(JSON.stringify(x) === "[3,1,2]", "the input was changed")

takeaway.key: Keep a sorted prefix and slide each new item left into place. O(n²) worst case, O(n) when nearly sorted, O(1) space, and stable.
mistakes: Using >= in the shift test and losing stability.
Writing to a[j] instead of a[j + 1] after the loop.
Forgetting to save the key before shifting, so it gets overwritten.
Calling sort() on numbers without a compare function.

dryRun.title: Partition [3, 8, 2, 5, 1, 4] around the last item, pivot = 4
dryRun.note: After one pass the pivot sits at index 3, its final sorted position. Everything left is smaller, everything right is not. Quick sort now repeats this on each side.

think.q:
const a = [3, 8, 2, 5, 1, 4]
const last = a.length - 1
let i = 0
for (let j = 0; j < last; j++) {
  if (a[j] < a[last]) {
    ;[a[i], a[j]] = [a[j], a[i]]
    i++
  }
}
;[a[i], a[last]] = [a[last], a[i]]
console.log(i, a.join(","))
why: Three items (3, 2, 1) are smaller than 4, so the pivot lands at index 3. The big items 8 and 5 end up on the right.
Only the pivot is guaranteed to be in its final place. The two sides are not sorted yet.

think.q: Always taking the last item as the pivot, what input makes quick sort slow (O(n²))?
opts: An array of all different values
An array that is already sorted
why: On sorted input the last item is the biggest, so every split is "everything" and "nothing". The depth becomes n instead of log n.
Fix: pick a random pivot, or the median of three.

think.q: Why is quick sort O(n log n) on average?
opts: A typical pivot splits the array into two similar halves, so there are about log n levels of O(n) work
It sorts the array before it starts
why: Each level of splitting costs O(n) in total, and balanced splits give about log n levels.
The risk is only an unlucky pivot, which is rare when it is chosen at random.

think.q: After one partition, what is guaranteed about the pivot?
opts: It sits in its final sorted position
It is in the middle of the array
why: Everything smaller is to its left and everything bigger to its right, so no later step can move it.
The sides still need their own sorting. That is the recursion.

think.q: Compared with merge sort, quick sort on an array:
opts: Sorts in place with only O(log n) stack, but has an O(n²) worst case
Always runs in O(n log n) and needs O(n) extra space
Is stable and needs no recursion
why: Merge sort does its work while joining and needs a helper array. Quick sort does its work while splitting and swaps in place.
Quick sort is usually faster in practice because it has low overhead, but it is not stable.

try.task: Write partition(nums). Use the last item as the pivot and rearrange nums in place so smaller items are on its left and the rest on its right. Return the index where the pivot ends up.
examples: const a = [3, 8, 2, 5, 1, 4]; partition(a)  // 3, and a is now like [3, 2, 1, 4, 8, 5]
try.hint: Keep i as the next free slot for a small item. For j from 0 to n - 2, swap a[j] into slot i when it is smaller than the pivot. At the end swap the pivot into slot i.

checks.t: the pivot lands in its final place
checks.verify: const a = [3, 8, 2, 5, 1, 4]; const p = partition(a); assert(p === 3 && a[3] === 4, "expected the pivot 4 at index 3, got index " + p)

checks.t: smaller on the left, the rest on the right
checks.verify: const a = [9, 4, 7, 1, 8, 2, 6, 5, 3, 0, 5]; const pv = a[a.length - 1]; const p = partition(a); assert(a[p] === pv, "the pivot is not at the returned index"); for (let k = 0; k < p; k++) assert(a[k] < pv, "left side has a big item at " + k); for (let k = p + 1; k < a.length; k++) assert(a[k] >= pv, "right side has a small item at " + k)
const a = [5, 1, 5, 2, 9, 3]; partition(a); assert(JSON.stringify([...a].sort((x, y) => x - y)) === "[1,2,3,5,5,9]", "items were lost or changed")
const e = [2, 2, 2]; const p = partition(e); assert(e[p] === 2 && partition([7]) === 0, "all-equal or single item")

takeaway.key: Partition puts the pivot in its final spot with smaller items on the left. Quick sort repeats it on both sides: O(n log n) average, O(n²) with bad pivots, in place.
mistakes: Forgetting the last swap that puts the pivot into place.
Looping j up to the pivot index, so the pivot is compared with itself.
Always picking the last item on sorted input (use a random pivot).
Thinking both sides are already sorted after one pass.

dryRun.title: 3rd smallest of [7, 2, 9, 4, 1]  (target index 2 in sorted order)
dryRun.note: We only follow one side each time. The work is about n + n/2 + n/4 + ... = 2n, so O(n) on average, while a full sort is O(n log n).

think.q:
function qs(a, k) {
  let lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1
  while (true) {
    const p = a[hi]
    let i = lo
    for (let j = lo; j < hi; j++) {
      if (a[j] < p) {
        ;[a[i], a[j]] = [a[j], a[i]]
        i++
      }
    }
    ;[a[i], a[hi]] = [a[hi], a[i]]
    if (i === k) return a[i]
    if (i < k) lo = i + 1
    else hi = i - 1
  }
}
console.log(qs([7, 2, 9, 4, 1], 2))
why: Index 2 of the sorted array [1, 2, 4, 7, 9] is 4. The loop only partitions the side that holds index 2.
It never sorts the whole array, yet it finds the right value.

think.q: You want the k-th largest item (k = 1 is the biggest) in an array of n items. Which index do you look for in sorted-ascending order?
why: With n = 5 and k = 2, the 2nd largest is at index 3 of the ascending array, and 5 - 2 = 3.
The largest (k = 1) is at index n - 1, the last one.

think.q: What are the average and worst case times of quick select?
why: Average: the range shrinks by about half each time, so the total is about 2n.
Worst: bad pivots shrink the range by one each time. A random pivot makes that very unlikely.

think.q: After partitioning, the pivot is at index p and you want index k, with k greater than p. Why can you ignore the left side?
opts: Every item there is smaller than the pivot, so the item at index k is not among them
Because the left side is already sorted
Because k counts from the right
why: The left side holds exactly the p smallest items, and k is past them. The answer must be on the right.
That "throw away a side" step is the same idea as binary search.

think.q: You need the median of one big array, once. Which is the best fit?
opts: Sort it, then read the middle
Quick select for the middle index
Binary search on the unsorted array
why: Quick select finds one rank in O(n) average. Sorting does more work than needed.
If you need many ranks, or the data keeps changing, a heap or a sorted structure is better.

try.task: Write kthLargest(nums, k). Return the k-th largest value (k = 1 is the largest). Duplicates count separately. Do not change the input array. Aim for O(n) average using quick select.
try.hint: Copy the array, set target = n - k, and loop: partition (with a random pivot swapped to the end), compare the pivot index with target, and keep only the side that holds it.

checks.verify: const x = [3, 1, 2]; kthLargest(x, 1); assert(JSON.stringify(x) === "[3,1,2]", "the input was changed")
const big = Array.from({ length: 20000 }, (_, i) => i); const t0 = Date.now(); const r = kthLargest(big, 100); assert(r === 19900 && Date.now() - t0 < 500, "wrong or too slow (use a random pivot)")

takeaway.key: Quick select = one partition step, then follow only the side that holds the target index: O(n) average, O(n²) worst, no full sort. For k-th largest the index is n - k.
mistakes: Mixing up k-th largest and k-th smallest (the index is n - k, not k).
Following both sides, which turns it back into quick sort.
Always using the last item as pivot on sorted data.
Changing the caller's array without saying so.

dryRun.title: Sort [2, 0, 1, 2, 0] with lo = 0, mid = 0, hi = 4
dryRun.note: Look at the first row: after swapping a 2 to the back, mid stays. The item that came from hi has not been looked at yet. Everything between mid and hi is still unknown.

think.q:
function sort(a) {
  let lo = 0, mid = 0, hi = a.length - 1
  while (mid <= hi) {
    if (a[mid] === 0) {
      ;[a[lo], a[mid]] = [a[mid], a[lo]]
      lo++
      mid++
    } else if (a[mid] === 1) {
      mid++
    } else {
      ;[a[mid], a[hi]] = [a[hi], a[mid]]
      hi--
    }
  }
  return a
}
console.log(sort([2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0]).join(""))
why: The three zones end up as 0s on the left, 1s in the middle and 2s on the right: 001122.
It makes one pass and uses no extra array.

think.q:
function bad(a) {
  let lo = 0, mid = 0, hi = a.length - 1
  while (mid <= hi) {
    if (a[mid] === 0) {
      ;[a[lo], a[mid]] = [a[mid], a[lo]]
      lo++
      mid++
    } else if (a[mid] === 1) {
      mid++
    } else {
      ;[a[mid], a[hi]] = [a[hi], a[mid]]
      hi--
      mid++
    }
  }
  return a
}
console.log(bad([1, 2, 0]).join(","))
why: This version moves mid after swapping with hi. The 0 that came from the back is never looked at, so it stays in the wrong place.
Rule: after a swap with hi, do not move mid. The swapped-in item is still unchecked.

think.q: While the loop runs, which part of the array is not yet looked at?
why: Left of lo are 0s, from lo up to mid - 1 are 1s, and right of hi are 2s. Only mid..hi is unknown.
The loop ends when mid passes hi, because nothing unknown is left.

think.q: What are the time and extra space of the three-pointer sort?
why: Each step either moves mid forward or moves hi backward, so the loop runs at most n times.
No second array is made. A counting approach needs two passes, and this needs one.

think.q: When a[mid] is 2, why is the answer to move it to hi?
opts: Because 2 is the biggest value, so it belongs at the right end
why: A 2 belongs in the right zone, which starts at hi. Swapping it there makes the zone one item bigger, so hi--.
The same idea sorts any three groups: "small", "equal to pivot" and "large".

try.task: Write sortColors(nums). The array has only 0s, 1s and 2s. Sort it in place, in one pass, with O(1) extra space. Return the same array. Do not use sort.
try.hint: Use lo = 0, mid = 0, hi = n - 1. While mid <= hi: 0 swaps with lo (both move up), 1 just moves mid, 2 swaps with hi and only hi moves back.

checks.t: the case that breaks "mid++ after hi swap"
checks.verify: assert(JSON.stringify(sortColors([1, 2, 0])) === "[0,1,2]" && JSON.stringify(sortColors([2, 2, 0, 0])) === "[0,0,2,2]", "check the swap with hi")

checks.t: only one colour, one item, empty

checks.verify: const a = [2, 1, 0]; const r = sortColors(a); assert(r === a && JSON.stringify(a) === "[0,1,2]", "must sort in place and return the same array")

const orig = Array.prototype.sort; Array.prototype.sort = function () { throw new Error("do not use sort") }; try { assert(JSON.stringify(sortColors([1, 0, 2, 1, 0])) === "[0,0,1,1,2]", "wrong result") } finally { Array.prototype.sort = orig }

takeaway.key: Three pointers split the array into 0s | 1s | unknown | 2s. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space. After swapping with hi, do not move mid.
mistakes: Moving mid after a swap with hi, which skips an unchecked item.
Using mid < hi and missing the last unknown item.
Sorting with sort() or a counting pass when one pass is asked for.
Not knowing the idea also covers any "small / equal / large" split.

flags: partition-algos: the try-it checks properties (pivot place, left smaller, right not) instead of one exact array, because many valid partitions exist.
dutch-national-flag: the "does not call sort" check temporarily replaces Array.prototype.sort. It restores it in a finally block.
quick-select: the try-it reference solution uses a random pivot, so the 20,000 item timing check is a loose bound (500 ms).
The dry-run tables are traced by hand (dry runs of concept lessons are not machine-run).
